Tell me about a time when somebody on your team told you that you were wrong.
Two thousand and nineteen. We had taken a fourth project and my site manager came into my office and told me the schedule was not real.
What did he say, exactly?
He said we would lose the fourth project or the third one, and that I had already chosen without knowing it. Then he asked me which one I wanted to lose.
That is quite a pushback. What did you do with it?
I asked him to say it again in the Monday meeting, in front of the other three engineers. It defused it, and it also meant I could not quietly ignore him afterwards.
And what happened?

We handed the fourth project back and lost the fee. It was my call, and I owned it with the client. What stayed is that people now tell me things earlier, which I can read in the morale and in nothing else. Does the program use panels for this, or is it always one interviewer?

This was two years ago, about six weeks before we were due to launch. My head of operations came to me and told me the plan would not survive the first week, and that two of his people had already said the same thing to him. So I asked him what he would do instead, which is a question I did not use to ask, and he had an answer, which was the uncomfortable part. What I did next is the thing I would want you to hear. I asked him to bring it to the leadership meeting and say it there. A private objection can be quietly ignored, and I know that because I had quietly ignored a few. An objection said in front of eight people cannot be. We changed the plan and we lost six weeks. What stayed is that people bring me bad news earlier now, and I would take that over the six weeks any day of the week.

People assume the behavioral question is testing self-awareness, and it is not, or not mainly. It is testing whether you can describe other people accurately. Everybody in that chair can describe themselves. Almost nobody can tell me what somebody who disagreed with them actually said, in their words, without turning it into a straw man. And here is the fastest way to fail it: an answer that is all I. If nobody else says anything in the whole story, then either you were working alone, which is not what we are recruiting for, or you have edited everybody else out, which is worse. One more thing, and it is free. The candidates who name the person who was right, out loud, by role, and do not soften it afterwards, are the ones the panel still remembers at the end of the day. It costs nothing and almost nobody does it.

A study of around ninety organizations measured something deceptively simple: how long a known problem took to reach the person who had the authority to decide about it. The average was eleven weeks. Not eleven weeks to solve the problem, eleven weeks for the problem to travel upstairs. What the researchers did not expect was the variable that separated the fast organizations from the slow ones. It was not size, and it was not the industry. In the teams where bad news moved fastest, somebody senior had visibly owned a bad result in front of everybody, in the previous year. There is a related finding about workarounds that is worth ending on. A workaround, in this data, is simply a problem somebody decided not to report, and the researchers point out that after about two years nobody in the team remembers that it was ever a workaround at all.
